title: Considerations for upscaling individual effects of wind energy development towards population-level impacts on wildlife
abstract: The expansion of wind energy poses challenges to policy- and decision-makers to address conﬂicts with wildlife. Conﬂicts are associated with impacts of existing and planned projects on wildlife, and associated diﬃculties of prediction where impacts are subject to considerable uncertainty. Many post-construction studies have demonstrated adverse eﬀects on individuals of various bird and bat species. These eﬀects may come in the form of collision-induced mortality or behavioral or physiological changes reducing the ﬁtness of individuals exposed to wind energy facilities. Upscaling these individual eﬀects to population impacts provides information on the true value of interest from a conservation point of view. This paper identiﬁes methodological issues associated when moving from individual eﬀects to population impacts in the context of wind energy. Distinct methodological approaches to predict population impacts are described using published case studies. The various choices of study design and metrics available to detect signiﬁcant changes at the population level are further assessed based on these. Ways to derive impact thresholds relevant for decision-making are discussed in detail. Robust monitoring schemes and sophisticated modelling techniques may inevitably be unable to describe the whole complexity of wind and wildlife interactions and the natural variability of animal populations. Still, they will provide an improved understanding of the response of wildlife to wind energy and better-informed policies to support risk-based decision-making. Policies that support the use of adaptive management will promote assessments at the population level. Providing information to adequately balance the development of wind energy with the persistence of wildlife populations.

## 1. Introduction

A drive to reduce emissions of greenhouse gases to mitigate anthropogenic climate change has boosted the innovation, development and application of renewable energy sources such as wind. All power generation, however, has environmental costs (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2011). Achieving acceptable environmental and social costs per kWh from wind energy therefore depends on the ability to address environmental and societal challenges. On the environmental side, populations of birds, bats, marine mammals and fish have the potential to be affected by the development of wind energy (Gill, 2005; Inger et al., 2009; Katzner et al., 2013; Schuster et al., 2015). Although this has so far not received much attention, terrestrial mammals may also be affected (Agnew et al., 2016; Skarin et al., 2015). The fast rate of wind-energy development presents the challenge of verifying the magnitude of impacts on wildlife and, if necessary,

constructing ways of mitigating these (Langston and Pullan, 2003; May et al., 2015). Negative effects on wildlife are generally perceived as a major conflict issue for wind-power development (Drewitt and Langston, 2006; Stewart et al., 2007).

In this respect, it is important to distinguish between the effects wind-power plants have on individuals and how these ultimately impact populations. Effects here relate to any change in the survival probability of an individual due to disturbance, barrier effects and direct injury or mortality. Impacts occur when the vital rates (reproduction, mortality, survival) for the population these individuals are part of are changed. Recent research has provided insight into the potential impacts of wind-power plants at the population level for various species (see Supplementary Information). However, it often remains difficult to assess population-level impacts due to the spatial scale and long-term monitoring data required for such studies. Currently, licensing of renewable energy developments is therefore routinely based on predicted

From a conservation point of view, it is crucial to assess the potential impact the development of a wind-power plant will have on the population at large. This, however, requires a good understanding of the definitions and requirements for appropriately predicting population-level impacts. Setting appropriate decision thresholds for regulation of the impacts of wind energy, and associated mitigation, are being suitably managed (Brownlie et al., 2013). The research question derived from this preamble, is how population impacts caused by wind energy development should be assessed. The objective of this review therefore is to provide an overview over how populations are to be defined, impacts measured and predicted, and how impact thresholds can be set and applied for decision making. Although the total load of all anthropogenic impacts in both space and time in the end determine the long-term fate of a population, this review focuses specifically on impacts due to wind energy development. The review was executed as part of the International Energy Agency's Task 34 called Assessing Environmental Effects of Wind Energy.

The review was based on an extensive desk research and literature review, where relevant literature was obtained through searches on Google Scholar, ISI Web of Science and the Tethys Knowledge Base (https://tethys.pnnl.gov/knowledge-base-wind-energy). Relevant search terms included: wind energy OR wind power, wind farm OR wind-power plant, onshore, offshore, population, demography, impact, effect, bird, bat, marine mammal.

## 2. Theoretical foundations for population-level consequences

The construction and operation of wind-power plants may affect individuals of a species through collision mortality, changes in behavior due to disturbance (e.g. moving rotor blades, noise, electromagnetic fields) and barrier effects, and habitat modifications leading to displacement. The nature and magnitude of those effects are highly siteand species-specific (Drewitt and Langston, 2006). The magnitude of such effects depends on the sensitivity of a species for disturbance and the effects this has on an individual's energy balance and consequently its fitness. Time and energy expenditure may increase due to stressrelated physiological responses, increased movement activity, and ultimately injury and death of either the individual or its dependent young. Increased energy expenditure due to barrier effects may lead to reduced fitness (Masden et al., 2010, 2009). Displacement from breeding or foraging habitat and changes in foraging efficiency may also influence an individual's energy uptake and ability to reproduce successfully. Recently, a study by Agnew et al. (2016) indicated physiological stress in badgers (Meles meles) nearby wind turbines.

Depending on the magnitude-of-effect these mainly behavioral effects have on the fitness of an individual coupled with the number of affected individuals, ultimately leads to reduced survival, reduced reproduction and increased mortality at the population level (King et al., 2015). Dependent on the demographic characteristics and spatial requirements of a species, these effects may result in significant population level impacts. Long-lived species with slow reproduction and high annual survival rates are particularly vulnerable to increased mortality (Dahl, 2014). The reduced breeding success due to displacement effects (e.g. abandonment of breeding sites) and/or loss of parents (through collisions or injury) may in turn affect population dynamics (e.g. Carrete et al., 2009; Dahl et al., 2012). It may however not always be clear whether the presence of wind turbines has significant population consequences (Dahl, 2014; de Lucas et al., 2008; Hunt et al., 1998; Madders and Whitfield, 2006), as this depends on the rate of direct mortality, the fitness costs of disturbance and on the availability of alternative habitat (Gill et al., 2001).

Within meta-populations, migration of individuals from good-

quality source habitat to lower-quality sink habitats may stabilize the demographic dynamics of a population (Dias, 1996). Wind-power plants located in good-quality habitat may change such sources into sinks (Dahl et al., 2012; Kirol et al., 2015). Sudden environmental change may uncouple the cues that individuals use to assess habitat quality (yielding lower fitness) from the true quality of the environment (Robertson and Hutto, 2006). This has been dubbed the ecological trap theory (Battin, 2004; Patten and Kelly, 2010; Robertson and Hutto, 2006). Ecological traps may occur when animals are falsely attracted to habitats with consequences of reduced fitness, survival and reproduction (Battin, 2004). Wind energy relevant examples include fish and their predators attracted to artificial reefs (Reubens et al., 2013; Scheidat et al., 2011) and bats misinterpreting turbines as trees (Cryan et al., 2014). Conversely, perceptual traps may occur when high-quality habitats are avoided when perceived to be less attractive (Patten and Kelly, 2010). Dependent on the sensitivity a species to disturbance and the vulnerability to mortality (Adams et al., 2016; Furness et al., 2013; Robinson Willmott et al., 2013), behavioral decisions (e.g. avoidance or attraction) may lead to functional habitat loss affecting fitness in individuals (May 2015). However, the magnitude of behavioral responses to disturbance does not necessarily reflect population-level consequences as such are dependent on the availability of alternative habitat and site fidelity (Gill et al., 2001). An example of this can be seen for the white-tailed eagle (Haliaeetus albicilla) at the Smøla wind-power plant where low levels of behavioral responses (Dahl et al., 2013; May et al., 2013), affect mortality and breeding (Dahl et al., 2012; May et al., 2010, 2011) but not population persistence (Dahl, 2014).

Sensitivity to wind-power plants may be related to age, sex or size classes, and specific life stages (e.g. migration, territorial/floater), as well as being potentially density-dependent. Consequently, the effects may not be homogeneous across a population but effect certain groups disproportionally affecting population dynamics in unexpected ways (Vindenes et al., 2008). The way in which the dynamics of a population are impacted by wind energy development also depends on the lifehistory strategy of the species of concern. While high-reproductive and often short-lived species (r-selection) are mainly affected through changes in fecundity, long-lived species often with lower reproductive rates (K-selection) are more sensitive to changes in survival (Sæther and Bakke, 2000). Fluctuations in the size of recruitment-driven populations are more strongly influenced by environmental stochasticity than survival-restricted populations (Sæther et al., 2004). Consequently, mortality for K-selection species will more likely be additive while r- selection species may compensate for collision mortality with a reduction in mortality from other causes or increased reproduction (Peron, 2013). Assessing additive effects may therefore prove to be more problematic in r-selection species. The extent of additive versus compensatory density-dependent responses to collision mortality is however not yet well understood, and difficult to study (Diffendorfer et al., 2015; Horswill et al., 2017; Peron, 2013).

## 3. Moving from individual effects to population-level impacts

Environmental assessment has been developed to ensure that the potential environmental consequences of plans and projects are taken into account before the project is licensed. Within the framework of these assessments, the planning and siting of renewable energy projects are guided by the precautionary principle in an attempt to carefully address wildlife challenges (Köppel et al., 2014). However, because uncertainty will likely remain, population assessment frameworks may be more suited to adaptive management approaches. Adaptive management approaches embrace the inherent scientific uncertainty and require tolerance thresholds of change and adoption of practices that build consensus through reducing scientific uncertainty to enable improved decision-making (Köppel et al., 2014). Clearly defining acceptable levels of population impacts and necessary mitigation to achieve the goal at the level of individual projects will be critical in assessing

how the development of wind energy can be reconciled with nature conservation laws, directives and policy (Cole, 2011). Where conservation goals are set at a landscape level, assessment of impacts solely within the spatial extent of a single wind-energy project will underestimate cumulative impacts and hamper mitigation (Kiesecker et al., 2011). It should therefore be clear that assessing population level impacts requires primarily an agreed working definition of ‘a population’.

## 3.1. What is the population?

When defining a population impact, it is necessary to determine the boundary of the population. Here we define a population as “a group of individuals from the same species which live in the same space at the same time and reproduce”. It is therefore necessary to define the spatial and temporal scale over which a population is considered. For conservation purposes, biogeographic or (inter)national scales over extended time frames may be the most appropriate. Alternatively, populations have also been defined as Evolutionary Significant Units (ESUs) based on genetic and ecological information (Crandall et al., 2000; Fraser and Bernatchez, 2001). However, these temporal and spatial scales would likely be less relevant for planning of wind energy development. Therefore, delineation of ecologically similar individuals co-occurring in space and time, based on multi-scale characteristics (i.e. long-term genetic makers, mid-term ecological tracers, short-term individual monitoring), may be more appropriate for short-to mediumterm management actions (Giménez et al., 2018). Taking reduced spatial scale for planning purposes to its logical conclusion: a windpower plant developer required to consider potential impacts of their project may define the local population of interest as those individuals within the wind-power plant development area (potentially including a buffer zone), within its 25–30 years life cycle. By contrast, the regulatory authority will likely be concerned with relatively larger spatial and temporal scales, e.g. understanding population impacts at the regional or national level of a country, potentially within timeframes up to 100 years or longer.

It is important to reconcile differing levels of spatial and temporal scales, providing insight into population impacts for all interested parties. This could be achieved through a tiered approach that allows scaling from local to regional and (eco-)regional to national (biogeographical) scales within intermediate timeframes allowing for recovery after decommissioning (e.g. 50 years) (cf. Kiesecker et al., 2011). When considering aspects of scale in the context of impact assessment it needs to be recognized that the definition of a population may affect the perceived acceptable change and impact. A change observed over a restricted scale, such as at a wind-power plant site, may be perceived to be large and less acceptable than that same change over a larger biogeographical scale. Similarly, changes that appear limited at the scale of a wind power project may have large impacts over a larger scale. Assessments at the regional scale may therefore be a compromise between the restricted view of a single wind-power plant site, and the large and onerous biogeographical scale assessment. Nonetheless, when defining the spatial scale of an assessment, the delineation of a population is unlikely to represent the true biological population but rather relate to assessment requirements, legislature, societal criteria or human perceptions.

In addition to defining the spatial and temporal boundaries of the population, it may also be important to consider the conservation status of the population and the regional importance of the population from a national or biogeographic perspective. Threatened or vulnerable species and species at the extent of their realized distribution range will have less resilience to overcome additional mortality or disturbance. Species that already are under significant pressure from other anthropogenic activities or climate changes may occur at reduced densities or have contracted ranges (i.e. shifting baseline or extent). A species' lifehistory strategy may further affect the way in which it potentially will be affected by development. Long-lived species with low breeding

output and habitat specialists may be expected to be especially vulnerable. Recovery from development, after decommissioning, may thereby also vary across species.

## 3.2. What is the impact?

Once a population has been defined, the nature of the impact must be determined. It is often necessary to consider how individual effects are manifested across time in order to predict the likely future impacts to populations. This may be to predict the likely future impacts of an already constructed wind-power plant or the impacts of development scenarios not yet operational. A variety of statistical and ecological modelling techniques can be used to predict impacts and cover a range of complexities, depending on data and knowledge availability (see Supplementary Information for different modelling approaches with examples). When assessing an impact, it is important to decide on how to measure changes to a population. This requires consideration of i) the parameters i.e. vital rates of interest, ii) the metrics to be compared and iii) the baseline against which impacts will be measured.

## 3.2.1. Choice of vital population rates

The population impacts of a wind-power plant predicted prior to the consenting and construction of the project, should provide the basis for post-construction monitoring to verify population impacts and reduce any uncertainty related to these. The prediction of population impacts requires use of demographic parameters or vital rates. Demographic parameters to target include, but are not limited to, population size or density (Rushworth and Kruger, 2014; Searle et al., 2014), population growth rate (Dahl, 2014; Schaub, 2012), mortality (Bellebaum et al., 2013; Carrete et al., 2009), breeding success or fecundity (Dahl et al., 2012; Ennen et al., 2012; Garcia-Ripolles and Lopez-Lopez, 2011), and survival rate (Garcia-Ripolles and Lopez-Lopez, 2011; Sanz-Aguilar et al., 2015). Deciding on the choice of these is contingent on the life history of the species, inherent variability, ease of measurement, and available data and associated monitoring effort. In order to develop predictive models, sufficient data are required to predict impacts with a sufficient level of certainty. It is therefore important to consider which vital rate has the greatest impact on population persistence and how is it expected to be affected by wind-power plant development for the species of concern (e.g. Garcia-Ripolles and Lopez-Lopez, 2011). The greater the natural variability or stochasticity associated with the parameters of interest, the less sensitive it can be expected to be to changes that may be caused by the development. The response time in vital rates to perturbations is also important to take into account. It is prudent to consider the ease of measurement of the parameter, because certain vital rates may be impractical to measure and therefore never be taken up as a method. Where the goal of monitoring is to reduce scientific uncertainty regarding mechanisms of impact then the hypotheses being tested may not be directly related to demographic vital rates. For instance, reducing uncertainty regarding flight height distributions is indirectly related to assessing changes to demographic rates using collision risk modelling.

## 3.2.2. Choice of impact metric

It is not only important to select the appropriate demographic parameter for assessment, but also the choice of metric by which any change will be defined. In some cases, the relative rate of change of a parameter may be a more suitable metric to assess, than the parameter itself. This is more likely to be the case if a historical baseline is not available and the chosen parameter, e.g. population size, is measured annually after the construction of a wind-power plant. Ability to distinguish the effects of the wind-power plant from other factors affecting the population trend is particularly important if the species is already declining. It is therefore key that the rate of change associated with the wind-power plant, i.e. a standardized measure, is used rather than the population trend or else any negative trend may be considered

unacceptable change.

When expressing the chosen parameter or rate of change, it can be described by the,

1. Magnitude (e.g. median, mean or other measure of central tendency);

2. Variability (e.g. range, variance or other measure of spread); or

3. Likelihood (e.g. probability distribution, AIC or other measure of statistical inference).

It is possible to present only the magnitude of change observed, for example by comparing the mean abundance measured pre-construction to the same measure taken post-construction (e.g. Baerwald and Barclay, 2009; Campedelli et al., 2014; Farfán et al., 2009; Garvin et al., 2011; Hernandez-Pliego et al., 2015). However, with information on both magnitude and variability it is possible to calculate the effect size, i.e. the significance of a phenomenon such as the mean difference in population metrics (e.g. Kirol et al., 2015; Sansom et al., 2016; Scheidat et al., 2011), and estimate the power or ability to detect change (i.e. type I and type II errors, cf. Maclean et al., 2013; Vanermen et al., 2015). In addition to using measures of mean and variance in assessing change, it is also possible to compare the relative likelihoods of a random variable to take on a given value (Fig. 1). The use of such an approach provides information on both the magnitude and likelihood of an event or change occurring and therefore provides additional context for decision makers. Such an approach is often taken (e.g. BalotariChiebao et al., 2016; Carrete et al., 2012; Dahl et al., 2012; McNew et al., 2014), where competing models are evaluated against each other using an information theoretic approach (Burnham et al., 2010). If adopting a probabilistic approach, it is possible to use techniques such as Monte Carlo simulation, a computational technique that uses random sampling to produce numerical results. In relation to birds and windpower plants, McAdam (2005) produced a Monte Carlo simulation of

the original Band collision-risk model (Scottish Natural Heritage, 2000) to include variation in flight height and the effects of wind direction and speed in the estimation of collision mortality of birds due to wind turbines. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service have also developed a probability-based collision risk model for predicting eagle fatalities that uses a Bayesian estimation framework (New et al., 2015).

Probability-based techniques have been under-used in the past, although their use is increasing (Schaub and Kery, 2012). Green et al. (2016) argue for the continued use of deterministic approaches and for decision makers to inform their decisions based exclusively on a measure of mean change where the assessment related to seabird colonies afforded statutory protection. An overreliance on deterministic approaches to measuring the effect and describing the impact, whilst statistically robust, does not inform an objective assessment of the inherent uncertainties and associated risks. This limits their utility for the purposes of risk-based decision-making, and by masking the inherent scientific uncertainty, deterministic results can provide a false sense of precision. It is also important to recognize that although statistical tests, with enough power, can detect change, the magnitude of the change and the acceptable level of change must be set by other means. It may be that the level of statistical power and magnitude of change required to exceed an appropriate detection threshold for monitoring an impact would not be an acceptable level of change in the context of the requirements set by nature conservation legislation. In such a scenario, decision makers would be expected to ensure the conservation of the population takes precedence over exposing the population to the risk of potential changes that can be monitored to reduce uncertainty regarding the magnitude of effect. Policies that promote highly stringent approaches to wildlife protection may therefore not be compatible with risk-based approaches to reducing scientific uncertainties through adaptive management.

## 3.2.3. Choice of baseline

When assessing an impact through post-consent monitoring, it is crucial to define a baseline against which a change can be measured. This is relevant when considering either predicted impacts or empirical data of realized change. Studies that seek to measure an impact post hoc often use comparisons Before and After construction (BA) or Control with Impact areas (CI), or a combination of these (BACI). The first method is to define a suitable baseline e.g. the population size 10 years prior to development and compare this to the population size after construction of the wind-power plant. This can be thought of as a Before-After study where After signifies after construction of the windpower plant. This method is often used, though the time frame may vary, but it should be noted that the choice of baseline may be subjective and can affect the interpretation of an impact. Winder et al. (2015, 2014), for instance, assessed the annual survival of female greater prairie chickens (Tympanuchus cupido) and lek persistence and male body mass in relation to a wind-power plant development and compared data from 2 years pre-construction with 3 years post-construction. Hernandez-Pliego et al. (2015) studied the effect of windpower plants in southern Spain on the abundance of nest sites over a five-year period in the Montagu's harrier (Circus pygargus). There are however limitations of before and after comparisons that do not include a control site, as they typically assume that there is no change in the environmental conditions and that all changes can be attributed to the wind-power plant development. However, Pérez Lapeña et al. (2010) developed a simulation method that incorporated environmental conditions and removed the need for a control site. They accounted for environmental variability between pre- and post-construction periods by re-defining the pre-construction data as a reference and predicting the expected bird count during post-construction using an environmental model. Such a methodology is extremely powerful, however it is rarely used as the quantity of data required to parameterize the environmental model is often a limitation.

An alternative method is to compare the future population size of the affected population i.e. at the wind-power plant site, with the future size of an unaffected control population (Control-Impact comparison design). This method uses space as a proxy for time, by assuming the unaffected site is similar to the wind-power plant site prior to development and therefore the baseline against which change is monitored is the unaffected site. A more rigorous approach is the combination of both above-mentioned approaches: the Before-After-Control-Impact (BACI) comparison design. Examples of studies employing BACI designs include white-tailed eagles (Dahl et al., 2012), golden plover (Pluvialis apricaria) (Sansom et al., 2016), grassland birds (Shaffer and Buhl, 2016), fish communities (Stenberg et al., 2015), and harbour porpoises (Scheidat et al., 2011). BACI approaches are in general recommended (Loss et al., 2012). Such a design requires monitoring population trends in the wind-power plant sites and a control site both pre- and postconstruction. Here the population trend in the control site is compared to the population trend at the wind-power plant site; overcoming the limitations of the previous designs. One difficulty with these approaches is the need for a representative control population that will respond to the environmental conditions in the same way as the treatment or affected population. This becomes particularly challenging when the drivers of species distributions are poorly understood such as in marine ecosystems. A modification of this concept is the gradient analysis. This method assumes that an effect will be graded from the site of the wind-power plant, to the unaffected control site, moving along a gradient of impact. Another, highly specialized approach to spatial analysis is presented in the MRSea modelling package guidance notes (Scott-Hayward et al., 2013). The MRSea analysis is ideally of systematic survey effort around the potential source of impact before, after and possibly during the impact period. A redistribution effect is confirmed by presence of a term in the model that specifies an interaction of event and locality (for worked examples, see Scott-Hayward et al., 2013). Russell et al. (2016) found that harbour seals (Phoca

vitulina) were displaced during pile driving. However, their analyses also indicated whereto and for how long they were displaced, which may help inform mitigation strategies. This approach may thus not only identify spatially explicit impacts of wind energy developments, but also render insight into the underlying ecological processes across a site.

An alternative is to assess the population size trends, and risk of extinction (for more information on the theory of extinction risk: Drake and Lodge, 2004; Engen et al., 2002; Inchausti and Halley, 2003; Lande, 1993; Ovaskainen and Meerson, 2010), from construction into the future within varying time windows (e.g. Carrete et al., 2009; GarciaRipolles and Lopez-Lopez, 2011; Rydell et al., 2012; Sanz-Aguilar et al., 2015). First, the population size immediately after consenting or construction can be compared with a future population e.g. after 25 years. The second variant of this method is to compare the population size at the outset of the wind-power plant development with the population size in the future e.g. after 100 years, when the wind-power plant has ceased being operational and decommissioning has restored the area, allowing for population recovery. In scenarios with no recovery, a shifting baseline effect can be expected should an impact occur. PVA that assumes a compensatory response through increases in the rates of either survival or productivity both during and subsequent to the period of effect would require density dependent assumptions. Horswill and Robinson (2015) report that while there is strong evidence for densitydependent population responses in some seabirds, there is considerable uncertainty about the form and strength of these relationships as they will generally depend on processes acting at a site-specific level. Density-dependent assumptions can give an indication of the time required for the population to reach its original size although shifting baselines arising from other effects, such as climate change may need to be considered. Given the likelihood that the baseline of population size will change in space and time, the key conclusion is that assessments must respond to the specific circumstances and needs. This points towards a case-by-case consideration of spatial and temporal scales, associated thresholds, and their use to compare non-impacted and impacted scenarios (but see D'Elia and McCarthy, 2010). As such, all impact assessments can lend themselves readily to adaptive management approaches, provided the inherent uncertainties can be meaningfully reduced through monitoring to inform the learning-by-doing cycle.

## 3.3. What is a significant impact?

When the impact has been determined and a change in the appropriate parameter detected, it is then necessary to determine whether the change, and therefore the impact, is significant and decide how this relates to what is considered an unacceptable level of impact. If a population is in good conservation status and the wind-power plant impacts are considered negligible, then it may not be immediately obvious why this step is required. However, as the number of wind-power plant developments increases, so too will the likely impact and at some point a management decision about the acceptable impact will need to be made. Although population impacts may be demonstrated through biological modelling and predictions, this conclusion in isolation may not always render a solid basis for decision making. For example, if a significant effect or likelihood has been proven (e.g. P < 0.05) but the actual effect size (i.e. the rate of decline due to development) is small, this may not require prompt action. Equally, when a large effect size is coupled to a high level of natural variability (and thus a statistically insignificant effect) the combined uncertainties may also not prompt action for the wind energy project under study. In addition, it may be unclear how population model forecasts should be presented in order to be useful to decision makers. Decision makers need to balance the potential impacts on the populations of sensitive species (environmental cost) with the socio-economic benefits (Addison et al., 2015; Johnson, 2013). Three kinds of thresholds can be distinguished: ecological,

## utility, and decision thresholds (Martin et al., 2009).

## 3.3.1. Setting impact thresholds

Ecological thresholds signify the values for a specific vital rate above which relatively small effects of wind energy development substantially changes the chosen metric leading to population decline. Use of habitat thresholds can provide an ecological proxy that assumes abrupt changes in the species-habitat relationships beyond which species persistence declines (Ficetola and Denoël, 2009; Swift and Hannon, 2010). From a wider perspective, ecological thresholds can also assess critical loads from cumulative impacts and the extrinsic factors in the wider countryside affecting local drivers (Groffman et al., 2006). Another kind of threshold is a utility threshold. These are vital rate values beyond which substantial changes in the management objectives for the population will occur (e.g. allowed harvest levels). Decision thresholds are conditional on, and derived from, the combination of ecological and utility thresholds, and are based on values of vital rates that should prompt specific management actions (Martin et al., 2009). Decision thresholds combine various thresholds, including also those of a socioeconomic nature (e.g. minimal environmental impact per kWh). As such, in decision making these three kinds of thresholds should be taken explicitly into account to ensure transparency with regard to how the thresholds were applied and combined.

Setting of thresholds at appropriate spatial and temporal scales is of importance. Generalized and static thresholds (e.g. 1% of natural mortality) will not capture the local dynamics of the populations, but eases management by giving certainty regarding the objectives. Conversely, local and short-term (dynamic) thresholds will shift continuously enabling more flexible management practices at specific sites, which may be more complex to implement (Groffman et al., 2006). The choice of threshold limits for a specific project with regard to environmental uncertainty and extrinsic anthropogenic impacts that are out of a developer's control (in decreasingly risk-aversive order: cautionary limit, target limit, critical limit) will also have a major influence on the overall impact on a population across drivers (Johnson, 2013).

3.3.1.1. Deriving ecological thresholds. Ecological thresholds are usually derived directly from the population trends and/or predictions. There are different ways in which ecological thresholds can be set. Most commonly used is to set “arbitrary” reference values such as significance level or quantiles. Although such thresholds are in a strict sense arbitrary, they are in fact often generally accepted in statistics (e.g. P < 0.05). Using quantiles also enable setting riskaversive (precautionary; e.g. 33%), intermediate (e.g. 50%) or risktaking (e.g. 67%) thresholds for decision making. Another approach is the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis (Ficetola and Denoël, 2009). The ROC curve plots the true positive rate (TPR, i.e. sensitivity) against the false positive rate (FPR, i.e. 1 – specificity) based on the cumulative probability distribution functions at various threshold settings. By assessing the performance of models for many possible threshold values, the threshold value for the environmental variable can be chosen that maximizes the specificity and sensitivity of that model. Finally, threshold values can be derived using methods specifically aimed at identifying abrupt changes or discontinuities in population trends (i.e. tipping points). Such methods include nonlinear regression (e.g. generalized additive models, polynomial transformations) and piecewise regression (Ficetola and Denoël, 2009; Swift and Hannon, 2010). In the early years of conservation biology, the concept of a minimum viable population size (MVP) gained momentum (Beissinger and McCullough, 2002). MVP is defined as the population threshold at which a declining population becomes a small population, with increased vulnerability to extinction (Caughley, 1994). MVP thresholds are empirical probabilistic estimates of population persistence over a stipulated period (e.g. by arbitrary convention at least 90% certainty of persistence for at least 100 years), or the evolutionary equilibrium population size where genetic

drift is matched by mutations (Traill et al., 2010). Green et al. (2016) propose to evaluate population-level impacts of wind-power plants on seabirds by calculating the ratio of expected population sizes with and without the expected effects on demographic rates of the wind-power plant at the end of its lifetime using a density-independent Leslie matrix model (LMM). This LMM-ratio approach is thought to be relatively insensitive to the assumptions made about the magnitude, variability and trends of demographic rates, because the same uncertainties apply to both the impacted and un-impacted scenarios. This approach however does not explicitly set impact thresholds. If the objective is to set an ecologically-based decision threshold, then accuracy is of importance, and underestimation of the threshold level could have profound consequences. However, even with sufficient empirical support, the utility of an ecological threshold must be interpreted carefully and in relation to the response variable and relevance to the management goal.

3.3.1.2. Deriving utility thresholds. An alternative method of setting an impact threshold is to look towards harvest theory (Runge et al., 2009). Utility thresholds relate observed, or predicted, population trends to losses the population is expected to be able to sustain. The most commonly used fixed-rate harvest strategy is known as Potential Biological Removal (PBR). Associated approaches have been used in the United States in the Marine Mammal Protection Act (Cooke et al., 2012; Lonergan, 2011, 2012) and also to assess the allowable take of migratory birds (Runge et al., 2009) and onshore wind-power plants (Bellebaum et al., 2013; Diffendorfer et al., 2015). PBR is an approach designed to ensure that populations be maintained at or restored to an “optimum sustainable population” (i.e. undepleted). It is based on a simple model of logistic growth of a homogeneous large population that suffers removals and thereafter recovers to a certain level of carrying capacity using a recovery factor (Cooke et al., 2012; Lonergan, 2011, 2012). The US Fish & Wildlife Service developed the Adaptive Harvest Management (AHM) concept for regulation of waterfowl harvesting. AHM is a systematic process for dealing objectively with four sources of uncertainty: environmental variability, partial controllability (of harvest), partial observability, and structural uncertainty. AHM aims at iteratively optimizing a number of different stochastic population models to derive the most appropriate regulatory strategy.

Acceptable Biological Change (ABC) is the name given to the threshold used in assessments of impacts on seabird populations from offshore wind-power plant developments in Scotland (Green et al., 2016). The approach uses cumulative frequency distributions in the specific form of posterior distributions from a Bayesian state-space modelling form of population viability analysis (Freeman et al., 2014). The threshold adopted by the Scottish Government is the average change for the impacted population that is within the range that is “about as likely as not” under baseline conditions. This is the difference of the median (0.5 quantile) and the 0.33 quantile of the non-impacted (“unlikely” impacted) population sizes, which in turn are taken from IPCC guidelines on the use of common language to describe likelihood (Mastrandrea et al., 2010). The threshold is informed by knowledge of likely future population sizes where the likelihood is driven by natural variation in life history traits of species. It allows for larger percentage declines to those species that are relatively more r-selected. The approach is unlikely to be appropriate if measurement error has not been accounted for in the modelling process using techniques such as integrated population modelling (IPM). Critics of ABC argue that more stringent thresholds should be applied that ensure no-net loss to populations afforded statutory protection under the Birds Directive. Also, the use of the average population change between impacted and nonimpacted scenarios was argued to provide a more suitable metric for that purpose (Green et al., 2016).

3.3.1.3. Deriving decision thresholds. Decision thresholds come in many forms. Probably most common are multiple-criteria and rule-based

thresholds (e.g. Lonergan, 2011; Mace et al., 2008). The IUCN red list uses a number of criteria to assess population status; these are based on reductions in population size, reductions in geographical range and probability of extinction (Mace et al., 2008). Depending on the likelihood for extinction within specific time frames, a population may be classified as critically endangered, endangered, vulnerable, etc. This, however, requires thresholds to be determined with sufficient accuracy to be able to assess threat level and prioritize conservation strategies. For offshore wind energy development, indices for potential vulnerability in seabirds have been developed that build upon the conservation status but also include behavioral factors (Furness et al., 2013; Garthe and Huppop, 2004). Such approaches are empirically driven and expert-based. However, in situations that data are insufficient or even lacking, meta-analysis of existing data from multiple sites can be used to provide more accurate parameter estimates and to reduce the uncertainty surrounding them. Thereafter, decision analysis can help in selecting among alternative choices using statistical information to shed light on the uncertainties involved (Mengersen et al., 2015). By contrast, participatory approaches include stakeholders to assess trade-offs in socio-economic and environmental objectives, using e.g. scenario planning (Addison et al., 2015). Such approaches are generally qualitative in nature, but can also include numerical and/or spatial components. Thus, expressed uncertainty can be assessed and taken into account in decision making by aggregating the consequence estimates of defined management scenarios (decision scores) of participants. Probably the most flexible approach to derive multi-criteria decision thresholds can be derived using Bayesian Belief Networks (BBN). Both empirical, also spatiallyexplicit, information and stakeholder ‘beliefs’ can be used to parametrize the BBN models; enabling flexible and participatory setting of priorities. BBN can both increase the conceptual understanding of population dynamics and simultaneously assess effects of various decision options (Bacon et al., 2002; Barton et al., 2012; McCann et al., 2006; Nyberg et al., 2006). Although BBN has been used widely in environmental and resource management, so far it has not yet been used with regard to decision making for wind-power plant projects.

It should, however, be stated that there are limitations of science and although it is possible to predict the likely change or describe the change observed and set thresholds based on biological and ecological theory, it will be societal acceptance that determines the final threshold value (Green et al., 2016). This has been frequently seen with hunted or fished populations with numerous instances where, despite scientific evidence to the contrary, the thresholds set according to societal values have led to ecologically undesirable declines in populations. On the other hand, any technique for setting thresholds that allows for change can be expected to raise objections from those who believe they do not provide sufficient protection for the population.

## 3.3.2. Incorporating uncertainty

Acknowledging the environmental and demographic stochasticity inherent to population dynamics is important when assessing potential impacts on species of concern. Even with the most sophisticated prediction models, these will never be able to fully capture all variability in observed population trends. All models will necessarily have their own assumptions, simplifications and limitations in order to predict the magnitude, variability and likelihood of an impact to occur due to wind energy development. In addition, the actual data such models are based upon may also be restricted in quality, and be biased with regard to accuracy, consistency, timeliness and completeness. From this perspective, it is of importance in all modelling exercises to not only evaluate the predictive power of a model but also patterns in residual (unexplained) variance. Any empirical uncertainty can to a certain extent be taken into consideration through bias corrections using mixed effect models or through parameter calibration using Monte Carlo simulations or Bayesian approaches. However, besides empirical

uncertainty, the influence of assumptive uncertainty (also known as model uncertainty) may be more difficult to evaluate. It will, therefore, be pertinent that in all situations the reasoning behind specific model assumptions is made transparent (Masden et al., 2015). This may include the spatial and temporal scale, choice of parameter/metric, assumptions on linearity and density-dependence, autocorrelative structure, etc. Sensitivity analyses and simulations assessing the potential influence of different sources of biases in the data and model assumptions may provide more insight in their respective influence on the model predictions.

## 4. Managing population-level impacts

Population viability analyses are being used by policy makers for identifying tolerance thresholds for potential change in light of potential effects, which are themselves subject to natural variation and other scientific uncertainties. In this context, understanding not just the magnitude of change, but also the likelihoods associated with different magnitudes has value by adding contextual information. Risk-based decision-making can use this information, especially when applied as adaptive management. Adaptive management is a structured framework to progressively reduce the scientific uncertainties associated with decision making is created.

A key consideration from a policy perspective is the reconciliation of precautionary approaches with risk-based approaches. This ultimately requires a balancing of competing principles. Wright et al. (2016) identify this as a key challenge for the success of marine renewable energy. In practice, however, the same challenges apply to all decision making where the impacts to populations are not certain. Approaches such as no-net loss are unlikely to be preferred by policy makers concerned with balancing risk with precaution, unless the tolerance levels of potential change are already being exceeded. Where nonet loss policies are applied, the utility of assessing population level impacts and reducing scientific uncertainty to improve future decisionmaking may also be limited. Where no-net loss is the goal, the focus of the assessment will be driven by the number of individuals thought to be affected, and not the estimated population impact and its associated uncertainties.

Policy makers seeking to establish thresholds will wish to inform their decisions with an understanding of population state through time and the extent to which potential impacts will change the range of outcomes. Where there are no precise ecological or biological thresholds that are deemed of relevance to the decision-making process, the levels of stringency applied in the adoption of tolerance thresholds ultimately reflects societal and political considerations. In this context, political decision-making at the spatial scale of nation states can be expected to be the dominant process governing regulated activities that impact populations of conservation interest. For instance, in the EU setting Favorable Reference Values (FRV) is thought to provide a quantitative reference against which progress can be measured and setting such targets is an important step. FRVs define the species range and population, or habitat area, at which the overall conservation status of the species can be considered favorable. However, how such thresholds are set is so far inconsistent and in part arbitrary (McConville and Tucker, 2015).

Finally, the extent to which project-based thresholds can ensure population perseverance at larger spatial and temporal scales remains unclear. It has been suggested that the impacts of renewable energy are small relative to other factors (Erickson et al., 2001; Rydell et al., 2012). However, rapid and large-scale utilization of renewable energy resources challenges our ability to anticipate (and subsequently verify) the accumulated impacts on populations from energy power plants and their related infrastructure over large geographical regions. Because most impact studies have primarily focused on species-specific impacts associated with single power plants, cumulative impacts on the environment at large are generally not considered. Populations, not in the

least of migratory species, are however under the influence of a variety of both environmental and anthropogenic stressors (e.g. climate change, pollution), that somehow must be taken into account within a cumulative perspective.

## 5. Conclusions

Policy- and decision-makers can be expected to seek new and improved approaches to managing the conflict between wind energy and wildlife as the scale of wind energy deployment increases and the risks to wildlife grow. Risk-based approaches are expected to be increasingly informed by assessments that upscale from individuals to population levels. This paper has reviewed how population impacts caused by wind energy development should be assessed. In conclusion, assessments should clearly define the extent of the population at risk, and identify the impact metric associated with a species' vital population rate. Dependent on the chosen baseline, significance of an impact can thereby be modelled and assessed against relevant thresholds. Population level impact assessments will enable adaptive management practices to mitigate the potential for inherent scientific uncertainties to polarize opinion on either side of the wind and wildlife conflict. However, this can only be achieved in the context of risk of change to populations being tolerated at levels that are sufficient to enable robust monitoring of the potential effects of wind energy. Societal tolerance of risk, and the techniques used to inform the necessary tolerance thresholds of change to enable scientific uncertainty to be reduced, may become a key determining factor for the resolution of wind and wildlife conflicts.
